We've had a couple of instances of time running out at critical
points in the middle of actions. One such example was a vote called to
effectively oust his prey. There was no block, he (predator) clearly
had vote control, however with 30 sec. left, the prey effectively table
talked to try to get the table votes (which would not have helped
anyway). Needless to say 30 sec. passes very quickly and the game ends.
No table win, and more importantly no final!

A similar situation: bleed at stealth for the oust. Prey has no
intercept on table or in hand (can't prevent or pass the bleed). Five
tapped minions' three wakes in hand. Spends the final 30-45 sec.
slowly methodically deciding which minions to wake with (and fail to
block). Time runs out as the third wake is being played. Again, no game
win, no final.

I know the judge has the right to add time as needed. Two things I'm
contemplating:

1. If time ends in the middle of an action, the action is *always* be
completed.
2. If players want to keep time themselves they can, but the judge
won't revel the reaming time until the round is complete.

I'm more aggressive on #1 and not too sure about #2.

Should #1 be a tournament rule?

If #1 is used, can/should a lifeboon be allowed? How about a SR after
that?

Thanks for your comments,

***JediMike***

In both cases, I'd have referred to one of the tournament rules (number
5.1, aka "Cheating"), which lists (intentional) "Stalling to take
advantage of a time limit" as cheating in a tournament.

If you/the judge felt that the player in either case was simply
stalling to try to time out, then that player's cheating by the rules.

(In this case, #2 is pretty clear-cut if the player acted as you
described; #1 less so, in my opinion.)

So in case #2, were I judging, I'd have asked that player directly:
"Was there any way your play could have prevented him from ousting you
with that action other than timing out?" And when he admits no, rule
him ousted and award the VP to his predator (as well as determining the
penalty for the offending player.)

(See also: 5.3, "Slow Play".)

While your stalling examples don't suggest that any change to the rules
are required, the GenCon So. Cal. experience got me thinking that I'd
dodged a bullet and that some very tricky timing issues could occur.

What if a player announces a bleed to take their prey's last pool? If
the prey says "no block" and then time expires, is the prey ousted?
What about deflections or major boon or life boon? Can the judge look
and see that the prey has a wake and deflect and then determine that
the action wasn't completed? Maybe a judge would ask all the players
if they had any other cards that they were intending to play? If so,
then the action wasn't completed. On the other other hand you wouldn't
want to give players the idea to play a forced awake just to declare
the action incomplete-especially if they wouldn't have thought of it
on their own.

Of course, all of my rambling can simply be covered by the judge's
discretion. If the judge says the the action is complete then the prey
is ousted!

We've had other variations of the rules on how tournament games finish.
We inherited "1 minute to finish your turn" but that was no good
because that 1 minutes is not your own minute (you don't have sole
control of how it is used).

Would a change to "finish your current action" be easier for judges to
handle? Would it introduce new problems?

I think it would be much easier to handle. I have supported this "fix"
before. However, it has a flaw: It does not address non-action ousts.

I was in a game once where I had some number of counters on Smiling
Jack, and I ended my turn (no actions or transfers) just to get an oust
before time ran out. I said "go"; my prey scooped his vampires; the
judge said "time"; I said "Good game", in that order. However, since
noone had declared him dead and he hadn't moved his pool counters, it
was ruled that he was still alive (hadn't finished untap effects.)

I think scooping your cards is a declaration of death, but that's in
the past and more importantly is not the issue at hand. What I'm
looking at here is, let's say he hadn't scooped? Perhaps he had just
"thought", instead, and that took 5 seconds? You have hard calls to
make, as a judge, under the current system--not to mention, it's
frustrating to a player to do what it takes to oust, and then have that
oust contingent on how fast your prey decides to process it.

For the sake of equal treatment for actions and non-action ousts, I
would propose that when time is called, that players play until the
next time a player actually has to initiate something--declare a new
action, begin a phase, play a master, etc. (Reactions to an existing
action or master wouldn't count.) So if you declare a Kine Resources
Contested, and then time is called, then you finish that KRC. When
it's done, you would normally either take another action or end the
phase, so the game's over. In the case of Jack, I had declared the end
of my turn, so my prey was already in his untap. He would finish that
phase (and die), beginning the next player's turn (and therefore ending
the game).

In short, this is exactly the same as saying "finish the current
action", except it specifies exactly when an action is over (when the
next action or phase would begin) and that it handles Anarch Revolt and
Dragonbound.

Just my two cents.

-- Brian

Had the other players' hands changed at all? It is up to the judge (no
slight intended against their judgement in the matter) but if the
player is clearly doing something that isn't changing the game state
and the judge determines that the purpose of the action is to gain an
advantage by using the time limit, then the judge is free to call it
stalling.

To say it another way, just because an individual action is legal and
no one is playing slowly, doesn't mean that there is no stalling. For
example, I would consider using a "search your library for a piece of
equipment" action with each of your 10 Embrace--even though you know
there is no equipment in the deck--to be stalling. The fact that the
Embrace were legally entitled to take the actions and the speed with
which the player took the actions do not automatically exempt the
player from being in violation of the stalling rules.

The situation you describe above is a clear one and easily resolved. It
is easily resolved because you state that the action has been
"announced". Scenarios in which an action's end is announced or
clearly identified can also be created. The current rules and the
"play till action completes" proposal both work fine when the details
are clear.

Just like it is sometimes unclear (and requires a judge to use his or
her judgement) exactly when an action ends, it is sometimes unclear
(and requires a judge to use judgement) when an action has been
announced or begun.

Why change the rules to just move the judgement from when an action
ends to when an action begins? There has to be some benefit.

There could be some benefit to it because I think it may be easier to
judge when an action begins. On the other hand, you kinda have to "be
there" to determine if an action has begun. Players may dispute what
words were actually said or not said at the never moment time is
announced. It may be impossible for the judge to figure out exactly
what was or wasn't announced before "time" was called. On the other
other hand, it might be easier for a judge to look at the game state
using the current rules to determine if an action is complete (cards in
players' hands, etc.).

Stalling is the only way a player can take advantage of "time" being
called. There is no way to make everyone happy in these scenarios; the
only thing we can do here is try to make sure nobody can make use of it.

>To steal an opinion from a friend of mine, in boxing when a boxer is

So in short, you feel that the action should be completed.

What about when the prey is at 2 pool and the predator has 3 more
minions? Igo's bleed completes, and now the prey is at 1 pool. By your
logic, we must now allow the predator to take a second action.

What about when the grandpredator has an Anarch Revolt on the table and
the edge, and the prey is at 1 pool, and the grandpredator has just
finished making his transfers, but hasn't said "Done" yet? By your
logic, we must allow the predator to enter his untap and immediately say
"Done".

So what if we revert to the old way, where someone got to finish their
turn when time was called? Well, THAT wasn't fair for a number of
reasons:

-- Additional information received allows you to tap out all your
minions bleeding or take other extremely-risky actions, since you no
longer need to defend

-- Stalling is actually MORE prevalent, since if your turns take a long
time, it is more likely the game will end on your turn and you'll have
One Last Go

-- ...and thousands more. The above two are more than sufficient to
remove the "finish your turn" rule from consideration, though.

All of the above just serve to point out that "time" is a line in the
sand that has to be drawn somewhere. "TIME MEANS NOW" is the simplest
option, and the "random time" idea mentioned above prevents anyone from
making effective use/abuse of it. And many times, simplest is best.

One final point: Look at the NHL. If the puck is not in the net when
the buzzer sounds, the goal doesn't count. That's a "time means now"
rule that has stood the test of nearly a hundred years... and you NEVER
hear the players complain about it, because it's as concrete as it gets.
The goalie could've been lying on the ice out by one of the faceoff
circles, but if that puck didn't get in, it's no goal... and all the
players accept it.

So here you go; If you don't get that last pool by the time "time" is
called, build a faster deck next time, get the players at your table to
play quicker, call a judge if you think they're stalling, do whatever...
but get that last pool sooner next time, and you won't have to worry
about it.

(Can you tell I have little sympathy for a game that takes too long as
it is? 2 hours is way too much for this type of game, honestly. The
game's primary failing is its length; anything that has the potential to
make the game longer I'm completely against.)

Given that some actions can take a very long time to complete, wouldn't
allowing the started action to complete even though time has been called
defeat the purpose of a time limit? For that matter, just let the game
play to completion. It's more or less the same idea because when
constructing rules, you have no idea how long a given action or a given
game will take.

Never mind the fact that as that last action resolves, everybody's
motivations have changed. For example, if I'm your cross-table voting
buddy and my prey is at 5 pool and yours is at 1, I might've been willing
to help you pass a KRC that did 1 to your prey and 3 to mine knowing that
I can probably pull off 2 pool damage during my turn. Now that I know I'm
not going to have a turn, why should I help you with your KRC? But what
if I'm at 3 pool and now your prey starts bargaining for my VP, but now I
want the .5 victory points and I think he's bluffing about having 2
Surprise Influence anyway...blah, blah, blah, blah....

Potentially long discussion ensues. Better to just let the game end when
it's meant to.

If the answer is yes, then you are assuming the player's lack of action imply a pass,
while in the absence of a time limit a pass would only be assumed for sure once another
event was announced. If the answer is no, it could very well be that player changed his
mind after time was called, and there's no way to prove it one way or the other.

a Life Boon, then time is called. At some point he decides to pass, he is not sure if that
decision was made before or after time was called. Since this decision is made only in his
mind, the judge would have to be a mind reader to see when it was made, and hence when the
'no pass' became an 'implicit pass'.

However, if you say the oust is not complete until everyone explicitly says so or another
event comes along to imply it, then you can always rely on physical events to make your
judgement.

It's not a downfall at all, Mike. There is a really easy solution to
this. Call a judge over. If you feel dirty doing this, take a shower
when you get home. ;)

I have almost never done myself, but that's what judges are there for!
The five year's worth of Origins tournaments (and the several non-Origins
tournaments) that I've run are what I use as a baseline for discussions
like this, and even granting that the talent pool at those tournaments are
*extremely high* (i.e. they rarely act like children that need
babysitting), I've had to make maybe two dozen end-of-game rulings total.

There's been a few times when I've been asked by players to come over in
the final few minutes and "watch the game", and when that happens, I know
what they're really asking me to do. Police it. So I do. And a few
times within those few times I've *suggested* (as Goudie puts it:) that
players speed up their play so that I don't have to call them on stalling,
and they almost always do speed up.

I've also been asked several times by a player to add time onto their game
due to stalling by another player, and I only do this when the stalling is
happening RIGHT NOW. So, if playerX calls me over and says playerY is
stalling -- and I agree -- I'll tell playerY as nicely as possible that he
needs to speed things up to make sure that he isn't called on stalling
again, and I'll generally add 1-2 minutes onto that table's clock, or more
if a discussion was necessary at that point. But if playerX calls me over
and says playerY was stalling 30 minutes ago, blah blah blah, I'll begin
to police that table at THAT point, but since I wasn't there 30 minutes
ago, I won't give that table any additional time.

This really all boils down to doing your best to follow the rules, and
following them well (sorry Raille!) but also using your common sense to
interpret and "judge" what has happened in a situation and what the proper
remedy should be.

available during normal business hours, for a price, s'what I hear... ;)
